prompt: How does a pull CDN get a file it has never seen before?

options.text: It fetches it from the origin on the first request at that PoP, then caches it
It returns 404 to users until you upload the file to every PoP yourself
It copies the file from a nearby user's browser cache over peer-to-peer
DNS resolves the request straight to the origin, which serves it uncached each time

explanation: Pull CDNs fill on demand: a miss is forwarded to the origin and the response is stored per its headers. Requiring an upload is the push model. CDNs never read browsers' caches. DNS only maps names to addresses; with a pull CDN the name points at the edge, which caches what it fetches.

scenario: A game studio ships a 40 GB patch at 18:00 on Tuesday. Millions of players will download it within the first hour, from every continent. The file never changes once released.

options.text: Push: upload the patch to the CDN before release so every location has it at 18:00
Pull with a 10-second TTL, so every PoP fetches the patch from origin on first demand
No CDN; scale the origin horizontally to serve every download directly
Pull with Cache-Control: no-store so players always get the exact released file

explanation: A large, immutable file with a huge predictable burst is the textbook push case: pre-position it so no PoP has to pull 40 GB from the origin at the moment of peak demand. A 10-second TTL would make PoPs refetch constantly, and every first request at peak pulls from the origin. Serving millions of 40 GB downloads from the origin is slow for distant users and extremely expensive. no-store forbids caching, so every download would hit the origin; the file is immutable, so there is nothing to keep fresh.

options.text: The response must never be stored by the browser or by any shared cache
It may be stored, but must be revalidated with the origin before each use
Only the browser may store it; shared caches such as CDNs must not keep it
It may be cached for a default hour, after which it is refetched from origin

explanation: no-cache means 'check before you use it', typically via an ETag and a 304. Never storing is no-store. Browser-only caching is private. There is no default one-hour lifetime attached to no-cache.

prompt: Which header set is best for /static/app.3f9a1c.js, whose filename changes whenever its content changes?

options.text: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable
Cache-Control: public, no-cache, max-age=31536000

explanation: A fingerprinted file can never change under the same URL, so cache it for a year everywhere and mark it immutable. no-store throws away all caching, whatever else is listed. private stops the CDN caching a file that is identical for everyone. no-cache forces a revalidation round trip before every use for something that can't have changed.

prompt: What is the most likely cause of the low hit rate?
scenario: An image service sets Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 on every image, yet its CDN hit rate is 15%. Responses include Vary: User-Agent because one code path once served WebP only to some browsers.

options.text: max-age=86400 is too short for images, so copies expire before they are reused
Vary: User-Agent stores a separate copy per browser string, so most requests miss
The public directive stops shared caches like the CDN from storing the images
CDNs skip caching binary image responses unless they are explicitly pushed to them

explanation: There are thousands of distinct User-Agent strings, so Vary: User-Agent fragments each image into thousands of cache entries. Normalise to a small set (or vary on Accept) instead. A day-long TTL is generous for this. public explicitly allows shared caching. Images are the most commonly CDN-cached content there is, and pull CDNs cache them on demand.

prompt: A cache revalidates with If-None-Match and the content hasn't changed. What does the origin send?

options.text: 200 OK with the full body and a new ETag
304 Not Modified with no body
204 No Content, since nothing changed
412 Precondition Failed for the matched tag

explanation: A matching ETag means the cached copy is still valid, so the origin sends 304 with headers only and the cache refreshes its freshness. 200 with a body is what happens when the ETag doesn't match. 204 means a successful request with no content, not 'unchanged'. 412 is for failed preconditions such as If-Match on writes; here the precondition matched.

scenario: A site serves English or French depending on a lang cookie. After adding a CDN, French users sometimes see English pages. The CDN uses the default cache key of host, path and query string, and responses have no Vary header.

options.text: The cache key ignores the cookie, so whichever language is cached first is served to all
The TTL is too long, so pages cached before the French launch are still being served
The CDN auto-translates pages into the PoP's local language before serving them
French browsers send no-cache by default, so they bypass the CDN and get English

explanation: The language changes the response but isn't in the key, so both languages share one entry. Fix it by putting the language in the URL path or adding the normalised cookie value to the cache key. A shorter TTL would only change how often the wrong language flips. CDNs don't translate content. Browser language settings don't change caching directives, and bypassing the CDN would reach the origin, which serves French correctly.

prompt: Which changes usually raise CDN hit rate without serving wrong content? Select all that apply.

options.text: Exclude tracking parameters such as utm_source from the cache key
Sort query parameters before the lookup
Add an origin shield
Add the session cookie to the cache key

explanation: Removing irrelevant parameters and normalising order both collapse duplicate keys for the same content. An origin shield lets edge misses hit a regional cache instead of the origin. Adding the session cookie makes every user's copy unique, which drives the hit rate toward zero.

prompt: What is the best approach for future releases?
scenario: Each deploy, the team purges /static/* so users get the new app.js and styles.css. Right after each purge the origin's CPU spikes and pages load slowly worldwide for a few minutes.

options.text: Purge more often, in smaller batches, so the cache stays small and refills gradually
Fingerprint file names, cache them for a year as immutable, and keep only the HTML short-lived
Set no-store on static files so users always fetch the latest version from the origin
Raise the static files' TTL so the cache refills less often after each deploy's purge

explanation: Versioned URLs make new deploys use new keys, so nothing needs purging and the old files keep serving pages that still reference them. Purging more often causes more cold-cache stampedes, however it is batched. no-store sends every request to the origin, making the spike permanent. TTL changes don't help because the purge is what empties the cache.

prompt: What does purge-by-tag (Fastly Surrogate-Key, Cloudflare Cache-Tag) let you do?

options.text: Invalidate every response labelled with a tag, such as all of one product's pages and images
Purge only the cached objects older than a given age, across all PoPs in one call
Push tagged files into every PoP in advance, so the first request is already a hit
Tag users into A/B test groups so the edge serves each group its own page variant

explanation: The origin labels responses with tags and one purge clears every object sharing a tag, regardless of URL. Age-based expiry is what TTLs do. Pre-loading content is push, not purging. A/B assignment is an edge-compute use, unrelated to surrogate keys.

prompt: Which statement about the CDN is accurate?
scenario: A news homepage is the same for all anonymous users, changes every few seconds, and receives 20,000 requests a second at peak. The team says it can't use a CDN because the page is dynamic.

options.text: Microcache it for 1–5 seconds; the origin then sees a few requests per PoP per second
They're right: a page that changes every few seconds cannot be cached at a CDN at all
Cache it for a day and purge the homepage on every change so it is always current
Move the whole site into edge functions, each with its own copy of the database

explanation: A shared response that changes every few seconds is ideal for microcaching: a few seconds of staleness collapses thousands of identical requests. Saying dynamic pages can't use a CDN ignores microcaching. A day-long TTL with constant purges creates purge storms and cold caches. Rewriting everything as edge functions is a large redesign, and per-PoP database copies would be hard to keep consistent.

prompt: Using the lesson's illustrative prices, why does dropping hit rate from 95% to 80% matter so much?

options.text: Origin egress quadruples, because misses go from 5% to 20% of traffic
The CDN charges a higher per-GB price on all traffic when the hit rate is lower
It doesn't; total cost depends only on total traffic, not on how much of it hits
It matters only for latency: misses are slower, but the cost of serving is the same

explanation: Miss traffic goes from 5% to 20%, four times the origin egress, compute and database load. CDN delivery is billed on bytes delivered to users, not on your hit rate. Total traffic is fixed, but how it splits between CDN and origin is what changes cost. Misses are slower, but each one also costs origin egress and compute, so cost does change.
